taxonomy.subtopic: Desmoglein autoantibodies, suprabasal acantholysis and intercellular IgG

questions.stem_html: A 52-year-old woman has painful oral erosions followed by flaccid skin bullae that rupture with gentle pressure. Histology in the accompanying panel shows suprabasal separation with basal keratinocytes remaining attached to the basement membrane. Which direct immunofluorescence finding is most likely?

options.text_html: Net-like intercellular IgG deposition throughout the epidermis
Linear IgG and C3 deposition along the basement membrane
Granular IgA deposition at the tips of dermal papillae
Linear IgA deposition along the basement membrane
Granular C3 deposition around superficial dermal vessels

questions.explanation_html: Pemphigus vulgaris is a type II hypersensitivity disorder caused by IgG against desmosomal cadherins, especially desmoglein 3 in mucosal disease and often desmoglein 1 in mucocutaneous disease. Loss of keratinocyte adhesion produces suprabasal acantholysis, flaccid bullae and a positive Nikolsky sign. Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular epidermal IgG in a reticular or net-like pattern.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Linear IgG and C3 at the basement membrane is characteristic of bullous pemphigoid, which produces tense subepidermal bullae and usually spares the oral mucosa.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Granular IgA at dermal papillary tips is characteristic of dermatitis herpetiformis and is associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Linear IgA at the basement membrane occurs in linear IgA bullous dermatosis.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Granular complement around superficial vessels suggests an immune-complex vasculitic process rather than desmosomal autoimmunity.

questions.educational_objective: Pemphigus vulgaris results from IgG-mediated loss of desmosomal adhesion, causing suprabasal acantholysis and net-like intercellular epidermal immunofluorescence.
